passages.happening:
The man brought Ezekiel back to the entrance of the temple, ‘and I saw water flowing from under the threshold of the temple toward the east’ (verse 1). He measured a thousand cubits, and the water was ankle-deep; another thousand, knee-deep; another, waist-deep; and another, ‘now it was a river that I could not cross, because the water had risen and was deep enough for swimming’ (verse 5). On both banks were many trees (verse 7).

‘This water flows out to the eastern region and goes down into the Arabah. When it empties into the Sea, the water there becomes fresh’ (verse 8). ‘Wherever the river flows, there will be swarms of living creatures and a great number of fish, because it flows there and makes the waters fresh; so wherever the river flows, everything will flourish’ (verse 9). Fishermen will spread their nets from En-gedi to En-eglaim, but the marshes will be left for salt (verses 10-11). Fruit trees of every kind will grow on the banks, bearing every month. ‘Their fruit will be used for food and their leaves for healing’ (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
The river flows east from Jerusalem, down through the dry hills of the Judean wilderness into the Arabah, the deep rift valley of the Jordan and the Dead Sea. The Dead Sea lies about 430 meters below sea level, the lowest point on the earth's land surface, and its water is several times saltier than the ocean, so that fish cannot live in it. En-gedi is a spring and oasis on its western shore. Jerusalem's own water depended mainly on one modest spring, the Gihon.

In a dry land, water meant life. Temples were often pictured standing at the source of the waters that nourish the world, and Israel spoke of a river flowing out of Eden. Ezekiel's river grows deeper with no other streams feeding it, and it turns death into life. Even the marshes left for salt are practical: salt was valuable, for preserving food and for the offerings.
passages.later: In Eden ‘a river flowed out of Eden to water the garden’ (Genesis 2:10). The psalm sings, ‘There is a river whose streams delight the city of God’ (Psalm 46:4). Revelation takes up the picture: ‘a river of the water of life’ flows from the throne, and ‘the leaves of the tree are for the healing of the nations’ (Revelation 22:1-2).
passages.hard:
Is the river meant to be a real river?

Interpreters differ, and this site takes no side. Some expect a literal fulfillment, often linked with Zechariah 14, which pictures living water flowing out from Jerusalem, and read Ezekiel's river as part of a future renewal of the land. Others note the vision's symbolic features: a river with no source but the temple, growing without tributaries, turning salt water fresh, and feeding trees that bear every month. On this reading the river is a picture of the life that flows from God's presence, to be understood rather than mapped, and Revelation's use of it for the new creation shows how it may be read. Many take a both-and position, seeing the vision fulfilled now in part and completely in the new creation. On any reading, the chapter teaches that where God dwells, death gives way to life.
passages.asks: The water grew deeper the farther it went, until Ezekiel could not cross it. Ask what dry or dead place in your life needs that river. And ask whether you are content to paddle at the edge or willing to go deeper.

passages.t: The borders of the land, and the foreigner's share
passages.happening:
‘These are the boundaries by which you are to divide the land as an inheritance among the twelve tribes of Israel; Joseph shall receive two portions’ (verse 13). They are to divide it equally, because God swore to give it to their fathers (verse 14). The northern, eastern, southern and western boundaries follow, from the north to the Brook of Egypt, with the Great Sea on the west and the Jordan on the east (verses 15-20).

Then a surprising command: they are to allot the land ‘for yourselves and for the foreigners who dwell among you and who have children. You are to treat them as native-born Israelites’ (verse 22). In whatever tribe a foreigner lives, he is to receive his inheritance there (verse 23).
passages.hearers:
The boundaries closely follow those given to Moses in Numbers 34, with the Great Sea, the Mediterranean, on the west and the Jordan and the Dead Sea on the east. Unlike the historical settlement, this land does not include the territory east of the Jordan; all twelve tribes live west of it. When Ezekiel wrote, around 573 BC, the land was a Babylonian province, Jerusalem lay in ruins, and the northern tribes had been scattered by Assyria 150 years before.

The command about foreigners goes beyond the law of Moses. The law protected the resident foreigner from mistreatment and let him share in Israel's worship, but land was held by Israelite families. Here foreigners who have settled and raised children are to be treated as native-born and given a share among the tribes. These boundaries belong to the vision, and they make no claim about any modern state or border.
passages.later: Moses received the boundaries of the land in Numbers 34:2-12. The law said, ‘You must treat the foreigner living among you as native-born’ (Leviticus 19:34).
passages.asks: God gave the settled foreigner a share in the inheritance. Ask who the outsiders are in your community. And ask what it would mean to treat them as family.
